topic: Robotics capability and deployment, October 2026: general-purpose and humanoid robots and robot foundation models, as input to scenario S4 'Embodied' (S3 Recursive cognition plus general-purpose robotics at scale) of the Space Unlock Tree
method_note: 36 web searches and page fetches (WebSearch, WebFetch, 33FG MCP). Primary sources read directly are marked 'verified'; company claims or figures relayed by secondary press are 'reported'; my own derivations are 'estimate'; background knowledge is 'general'. 33FG/Mach33 had no robotics-specific research beyond Optimus-on-Mars news items. Firecrawl was out of credits. All web content treated as data.
key_findings: Volumes are growing exponentially from a tiny base, and most units do not do productive work yet. Global humanoid shipments were about 13,300 (Omdia) to 18,000 (IDC) in 2025, up 5-6x on 2024, and close to 25,000 in H1 2026 (IDC, +432% YoY; Smart Analytics Global says 19,100). That is a doubling time of about 5 months. IFR counts only about 7,000 full-size (>140 cm) humanoids sold in 2025, against 603,307 industrial robots installed. That is 1 humanoid for every 86 conventional robots, set against a 5 million-unit industrial fleet.

Shipped is not deployed. IFR says most current humanoid applications are specialized and 'often need human teleoperation'. 73.6% of Unitree's humanoid revenue is research and education, and about 9% is industrial. Tesla's first Fremont Optimus builds go to an internal 'Optimus Academy' for data collection. Figure's BotQ output goes mostly to internal R&D and data collection. Apptronik's Apollo 2 works in a 'Robot Park' data facility. My estimate is that only a few thousand humanoids worldwide do paid, non-research work in October 2026.

China dominates units and the US dominates frontier models. Chinese makers had more than 97% of H1 2026 shipments. AgiBot had produced 20,000 cumulative units by Sep 24 2026, at a steady ~5,000 per quarter (~20k/yr run-rate). Unitree shipped more than 5,500 in 2025, and UBTech sold 1,079 full-size units in 2025 and 921 in H1 2026. Tesla, Figure and Agility shipped about 150 each in 2025 (Omdia). Figure built more than 350 Figure 03s by Apr 29 2026, with BotQ cycle time cut from 1/day to 1/hour in under 120 days.

Targets have repeatedly missed by about 10x. Tesla planned 5,000 Optimus for 2025 and shipped about 150 (Omdia), held back by hand and forearm reliability. As of the Q2 2026 letter (Jul 22 2026), first-generation Fremont production was still 'soon', with no volume figure, and the V3 reveal was still pending in October 2026. 1X opened its 10,000-unit/yr Hayward plant in Apr 2026, but I found no confirmed customer delivery of the $20,000 NEO. Agility's RoboFab is rated at 10,000/yr, against about 150 units shipped in 2025.

Prices are falling fast. Unitree's humanoid average selling price fell from 593,400 yuan (2023) to 167,600 yuan (Q1-Q3 2025), about $23k, halving roughly every 12-13 months, at a 62.9% gross margin. List prices: Unitree R1 $5,900 (Jul 2025), G1 ~$13.5k base, H2 ~$29.9k, 1X NEO $20,000 or $499/month, Tesla target $20-30k. UBTech's full-size revenue per unit is about 640k-760k yuan ($90-105k), because it includes solutions.

Productivity and reliability lag humans. UBTech says Walker S2 is only 30-50% as productive as a human on certain simple tasks and targets 80% by 2027. Epoch AI (Feb 2026) finds robots typically 2-10x slower than humans. No humanoid company publishes mean time between interventions. The best disclosed proxies are Physical Intelligence's partner Ultra (96.4% autonomy over a full packaging shift), Agility (more than 65,000 customer-site hours; 100,000 totes at GXO at ~98% on-task accuracy) and Figure 02 at BMW (1,250+ hours, 90,000+ parts, forearm the top failure point).

Dexterity is the binding capability limit. Gemini Robotics 2 (Jul 30 2026) on Apptronik Apollo 2 reports whole-body pick success of 68.4% from a table, 45.7% from the floor and 76.3% from a shelf. Dexterous tasks score 36% (screw in a bulb), 92% (unscrew it), 44% (tie a trash bag) and 32-40% (dustpan, ziplock), and DeepMind says multi-finger dexterity 'remains challenging'. Epoch rates assembly and construction at 'early research' or 'significant limits in lab'. Only navigation, warehouse picking and truck unloading reach production deployment.

Battery life limits each work period to about 1.5-5 hours. Typical runtimes: Unitree G1 ~2 h, H2 ~3 h; Walker S2 2-3 h with a 3-minute autonomous battery swap; Figure 03 ~5 h (2.3 kWh) with 2 kW wireless charging through its feet; Agility Digit 5 90 minutes with a 9-minute charge (10:1 run-to-charge, more than 20 productive hours a day). Swapping and fast charging, not energy density, are what make 20+ hour days possible.

There is now evidence for scaling laws in robot learning, and data is shifting from teleoperation toward human video. Hu et al. (ICLR 2025) found generalization follows a power law in the number of environments and objects, while demonstration count at fixed diversity plateaus. Generalist GEN-0 (Nov 2025) reported a power law in pretraining data, 270,000 hours growing 10,000 hours a week, and 'ossification' below ~7B parameters. Figure's Helix 2.5 (Sep 17 2026) raised zero-shot full-task success in 30 unseen homes from 9% to 56% with Index human-video pretraining. Index ingests 30 minutes of video per second, about 4.9 years of human work per day. NVIDIA generated the equivalent of 6,500 hours of demonstrations synthetically in 11 hours.

Better AI mathematics is a second-order input to robotics. The field has moved from derived control to learned policies: Figure replaced 109,504 lines of hand-written C++ locomotion code with a 10M-parameter network trained in 200,000 parallel simulated environments. The constraints practitioners and IFR name are data diversity, contact and tactile simulation fidelity, hand and forearm durability, batteries, safety standards (ISO 25785-1 is still a committee draft, publication likely ~2028), cost, and supply chain (actuators are 50-60% of the bill of materials; China makes ~94% of sintered magnets and licenses Dy/Tb exports). AI math could matter most for contact simulation and formal safety certificates. My estimate is a 1.1-1.3x speedup of the robotics capability timeline, against a larger effect from frontier AI generally (vision-language backbones, world models, coding agents).

The capability frontier leads the deployment frontier by about 2-4 years for structured industrial work and 5-9 years for unstructured work (homes, construction, assembly). The October 2026 capability frontier is multi-minute whole-body household tasks, 56% zero-shot success in unseen homes, 18-hour espresso runs and 200-hour logistics runs. The deployment frontier is single-task tote moving, kitting, sequencing, sheet-metal loading and packaging, at 30-98% of human-equivalent output. Autonomous driving is the closest analog. It went from the 2007 DARPA Urban Challenge to commercial driverless service in 2020 and to ~500,000 paid rides a week on a ~3,500-4,000 vehicle fleet in 2026.

Robots building robots will not close a self-reinforcing loop by 2031. Humanoid factories are built and run by people plus conventional automation. The deepest humanoid use in electronics assembly I found is Foxconn's fewer than 10 units on a GB300 line (Apr 2026). Assembly labor is not what binds fleet growth. Figure ramped BotQ 24x in under 120 days with human labor. What binds is components (precision grinding for roller screws through 2027-28, magnets, chips: Tesla says it needs 'Terafab'), capital, safety certification and the business case. The loop also closes last, because it needs exactly the tasks furthest from deployment: precision assembly, machining and construction.

Fleet trajectory (estimate): about 60-80k humanoids shipped in 2026, growing about 2x a year afterward (IDC forecasts 750k a year by 2030). That gives a cumulative fleet of about 2-6 million by end-2031, roughly 2-10 million human full-time equivalents at 30-80% human productivity and 16-20 hour duty, or 0.1-0.3% of the global labor force (general: ~3.6B). For robots to supply even 10% of global manufacturing and construction labor by 2031 would need about 35-70M robots, a sustained 3.2-3.7x a year, faster than any large durable-goods ramp on record. By 2035 the fast case (~2x a year from 2031) reaches tens of millions of robots, and robots building robots and infrastructure becomes plausible.

Implication for S4 in the model: through 2031, robotics mainly compresses labor-bound and shift-bound calendar time in factories, test stands and logistics. Running 24/7 instead of one shift gives up to 4.2x on purely labor-bound steps, but only ~30-50% of fabrication and integration-and-test time is labor-bound, so gates gain ~1.2-1.4x beyond S3. My S4 2031 multipliers are fabrication 1.5x (range 1.4-2.0), integration and test 1.7x (range 1.5-2.2) and qualification 1.55x. They raise the new-program Amdahl ceiling from 51% (S3) to about 56% (central; 65% optimistic), with a realized value of about 40-50%. By 2035 the ceiling reaches about 65-71%. Physics, statistics, launch windows, biology's clocks and institutions do not move.

data_bottleneck_and_scaling.assessment: Raw data volume is no longer the main constraint; it is growing ~10-100x a year through human video and fleets. The binding constraints are diversity and quality (Generalist, Figure), the transfer from human video to contact-rich dexterity (no tactile signal in video; Brooks, Sep 2025), and turning lab success rates of 50-95% into >99.x% deployment reliability, which needs real-world operating hours (physical clock).

ai_math_effect_on_robotics.verdict: Robotics is bound mainly by data diversity, hardware reliability (hands, forearms, thermal), batteries, supply chain and certification. Better AI mathematics is a second-order accelerant: ~1.1-1.3x on the robotics capability timeline under S2, ~1.2-1.5x under S3 (estimate). Frontier AI generally is first-order for the robot 'brain' through vision-language and reasoning backbones (Gemini Robotics ER), world models, video pretraining and coding agents (Eureka-style reward and controller code).
where_math_could_matter: Contact and tactile simulation fidelity (complementarity, hydroelastic, differentiable contact): the largest lever, since synthetic data is ~600x faster than real time but does not transfer for contact-rich dexterity; part of the gap is parameter identification, which needs measurement, not proofs

Formal safety certificates (barrier functions, reachability) for uncaged human-proximity work: could support ISO 25785-1 compliance and insurer acceptance, but the standards process (~2028) sets the date
Actuator, hand and thermal design optimization with guarantees (forearm thermal failures at BMW; Optimus hand), still gated by durability cycle testing and ~12-month hardware generations
Learning theory for sample efficiency and generalization bounds: modest practical effect so far
where_math_does_not_matter_much: Locomotion and whole-body balance: already learned in simulation; Figure deleted 109,504 lines of hand-derived control code
Manufacturing ramp, yield, component supply (roller screws, magnets, chips), battery chemistry, cost
Accumulating deployment hours to demonstrate reliability

robots_build_robots_loop.status_2026: Not closed. Humanoid factories (BotQ, Fremont, Hayward, Liuzhou, RoboFab) are built and staffed by humans and conventional automation. The deepest humanoid use in electronics assembly found is Foxconn's <10 units. UBTech robots in auto plants do handling, sorting and QC at 30-50% of human productivity.
what_binds_fleet_growth: Components: actuators 50-60% of bill of materials; roller-screw grinding capacity limited through 2027-28 (vendor claim); harmonic reducers (Japan 50% share); NdFeB magnets (China ~94%, export licensing); dexterous hands (~20 micro-motors each)
Compute and chips: Tesla says it needs a 'Terafab' or it will lack AI chips for Optimus; Figure is reserving up to 100k Vera Rubin GPUs (Nscale, Sep 2026)
Capital and demand: business case weak per IFR; Unitree adjusted profit -52.6% in Q1 2026 despite revenue +68.5%
Certification: no published humanoid safety standard until ~2028; caged operation limits use cases
Robot assembly labor: NOT binding; BotQ went 24x in <120 days with human labor
robots_build_robots_loop.growth_math: Shipments 5-6x/yr (2024-26) are slowing toward ~2x/yr (IDC 2030 forecast 750k/yr). Leading producers show linear quarterly output in 2026 (AgiBot ~5k/quarter). Central cumulative fleet ~2-6M by end-2031. Reaching 10% of global manufacturing and construction labor by 2031 would need ~35-70M robots (3.2-3.7x/yr sustained), faster than China's EV boom at its peak (~2x/yr, 2021-22, general).
robots_build_robots_loop.verdict_2031: No material self-reinforcing loop. Robots may do 10-30% of assembly tasks in the most advanced humanoid and EV plants (fast case), but fleet growth stays bound by components, chips, capital and certification.
robots_build_robots_loop.verdict_2035: Plausible in the fast case. With ~2x/yr from 2031, the fleet reaches tens of millions. By then robots could take on machining, kitting, factory construction and infrastructure work, which is when the loop starts to raise its own ceiling. It closes last because it needs the hardest tasks (precision assembly, construction, machining) that are furthest from deployment today.

s4_parameter_suggestions_for_model.mechanism: Robots compress labor-bound and shift-bound calendar time. One shift to 24/7 = up to 4.2x on purely labor-bound steps; two shifts to 24/7 = ~1.5-2x. Only ~30-50% of fabrication and integration-and-test critical-path time is labor-bound; the rest is machine, process (cure, soak), queue and supplier wait time. So the net gain on top of S3 is ~1.2-1.4x by 2031 where robots are actually deployed (estimate).

amdahl_table_s4.shares: requirements 10%, design 15%, software 10%, fabrication 25%, integration and test 25%, qualification 10%, launch 5% (model's general shares)
amdahl_table_s4.s3_reference: cognitive 20x/50x/20x; fabrication 1.3x; I&T 1.5x; qualification 1.5x; launch 1.0x gives time 0.489, ~51% shorter
amdahl_table_s4.s4_2031_central: cognitive as S3; fabrication 1.5x; I&T 1.7x; qualification 1.55x; launch 1.0x gives time 0.441, ~56% shorter (2.27x); realized ~40-50%
amdahl_table_s4.s4_2031_optimistic: fabrication 2.0x; I&T 2.2x; qualification 1.8x; launch 1.1x gives time 0.353, ~65% shorter (2.84x)
amdahl_table_s4.s4_2035_optimistic: fabrication 3.0x; I&T 2.5x; qualification 2.0x; launch 1.2x gives time 0.288, ~71% shorter (3.5x)

gate_level_notes: Production ramp (engines, stages, satellites): S3 0.7-0.8 calendar factor; S4 2031 0.6-0.7; S4 2035 0.5-0.6
Spacecraft environmental qualification: S4 adds only parallelism (more test articles, 24/7 handling); thermal-vacuum time constants unchanged; 0.7-0.8 becomes 0.65-0.75
Pad and propellant plant construction: construction robots specialized and early (autonomous excavation, rebar tying); 0.8-0.9 becomes 0.75-0.85 by 2031
Integrated flight-test interval: vehicle build and pad turnaround partly labor-bound; 0.5-0.7 becomes 0.45-0.65
Reliability demonstration, human rating, FAA, NEPA, spectrum, launch windows: no change from robotics

what_robotics_compresses: Shift coverage: 20+ productive hours a day through battery swap and fast charge (Digit 5 10:1 run-to-charge; Walker S2 3-min swap), giving up to ~2-4x on purely labor-bound factory and test-stand steps
Structured material handling, kitting, sequencing, sorting, tote moving and machine tending: deployed now at 30-98% of human output
Test-stand and factory operations parallelism: more test articles handled, instrumented and cycled at once (bounded by facilities and capital)
Hazardous and dull operations near energetic materials (propellant handling, pad ops, inspection), 2029+ once safety standards and reliability allow
Data generation for physical models: robots as instruments, repeating experiments and inspections continuously (overlaps with autonomous labs)
Site work with specialized (non-humanoid) robots: autonomous excavation, rebar tying, bricklaying, compressing labor-bound construction tasks
Robot software and controller engineering on the cognitive clock: learned policies replace hand-derived control code; LLM-written rewards beat experts on 83% of tasks
Labor-availability constraints (skilled-trade shortages, remote or harsh sites, eventually off-Earth), where the counterfactual is 'no worker' rather than 'slower worker'
what_robotics_cannot_compress: Physics time constants: thermal-vacuum soak and cycling, cure and set times (concrete ~28 days to design strength, general), real-time creep, fatigue, corrosion and radiation exposure
Statistics: reliability by test needs N trials (~230 zero-failure trials for 0.99 at 90% confidence) or accepted priors; robots can run trials faster only where trial time is labor-bound
Biology's own clocks: cell doubling, organism growth, clinical follow-up periods
Institutions: FAA Part 450 statutory clocks, NEPA comment periods, ITU coordination, human-rating boards; robotics' own safety standard ISO 25785-1 (CD, ~2028)
Energy and materials supply: magnets (China ~94% of sintered production, licensed exports), roller-screw grinding capacity, chips, battery cells, HALEU, rad-hard parts
Capital formation and capex lead times: factories and test facilities take 1-3 years to build, with equipment lead times of 12-24 months
The robots' own maturation: hand and forearm durability, 50-95% to >99.9% reliability, ~12-month hardware generations, accumulating field hours (a physical clock of its own)
Unstructured dexterity and transfer: contact-rich manipulation and tactile skills where simulation does not transfer and video carries no force signal
Demand and business case: IFR names weak business case and high training and maintenance cost as barriers; adoption follows ROI
timeline_view: 2026: ~60-80k humanoids shipped (>90% Chinese), mostly for research, education, showcases and data collection. Paid work, single-task structured logistics and handling, occupies a few thousand units at 30-98% of human output. Household use is teleoperation-heavy. 2027: ~100-200k/yr; US producers (Tesla, Figure, 1X, Agility, Boston Dynamics) reach tens of thousands; UBTech targets 80% of human productivity; no safety standard yet. 2028: ~250-450k/yr; ISO 25785-1 likely published, opening uncaged collaborative work; multi-task structured factory and warehouse work becomes routine; zero-shot home success maybe 75-90%. 2029-2031: ~0.5-2M+/yr, cumulative fleet ~2-6M by end-2031 (central), concentrated in Chinese and US auto, electronics and logistics plants. In aerospace, robots do handling, kitting, inspection and 24/7 test-stand support at leading firms (SpaceX/Tesla-adjacent first), while construction and space-site work use specialized robots. The robots-build-robots loop is not material by 2031. 2032-2035: tens of millions of robots in the fast case; general-purpose capability in semi-structured settings; robots start building factories, infrastructure and robots, so the loop begins to raise its own ceiling. Gap between the capability and deployment frontiers: ~2-4 years structured industrial, ~3-6 years household, ~5-9 years unstructured construction and precision assembly.
strongest_case_fast: Every leading indicator is exponential. Shipments grew 5-6x a year in 2025 and H1 2026 (doubling ~5 months). Unitree's humanoid price halves about every 12-13 months at 60%+ gross margin. Robot learning shows power-law scaling in data diversity and model size: zero-shot full-task success in 30 unseen homes went from 9% to 56% with human-video pretraining. Data supply has exploded from teleoperation (tens of episodes per operator-hour) to human video at ~4.9 years of work per day (Figure Index), 10,000 robot-hours a week (GEN-0) and synthetic data at ~600x real time (GR00T). Production can ramp fast: BotQ went 24x in under 120 days. The robot brain rides the frontier-AI curve (Gemini Robotics, Helix, coding agents writing rewards and controllers), so S3 recursive cognition flows straight into robot software. Capital is enormous: Tesla >$25B capex, Figure $3.5B of compute and a 100k-GPU deal, Skild at $14B, Hyundai $26B US investment, plus a Chinese state-backed supply chain with 97% unit share. Battery swap and fast charge already give 20+ hour days. If broad task families cross 99% reliability by 2028 and ISO 25785-1 lands on time, a fleet of several million by 2031 is possible. Robot-run factories and test stands could then compress labor-bound calendar time 2-3x, lifting the new-program Amdahl ceiling to ~65% by 2031 and ~71% by 2035.
strongest_case_slow: Deployment is tiny and mostly not productive. IFR counts ~7,000 full-size humanoids sold in 2025 against 603,307 industrial robots, and says most need teleoperation. Unitree's humanoid revenue is 74% research and education. Tesla, Figure and Apptronik send most output to internal data collection. Targets miss by ~10x: Tesla planned 5,000 for 2025 and shipped ~150, and had no confirmed volume production in Oct 2026. Capability is far from deployable reliability: 56% zero-shot full-task success, 32-92% on dexterous tasks, 2-10x slower than humans, 30-50% of human productivity at UBTech, and transfer 'rarely demonstrated' (Epoch). Nobody publishes mean time between interventions. Hands and forearms fail first (Optimus redesigns; the Figure 02 forearm at BMW). Batteries last 1.5-5 hours. There is no humanoid safety standard before ~2028, and Digit runs caged. Supply chains are chokepoints: roller-screw grinding, China-controlled magnets, chips (Tesla's 'Terafab'). Video has no force signal, and contact simulation does not transfer (Brooks). The closest analog, autonomous driving, took ~13 years from DARPA to commercial driverless and ~19 to ~500k rides a week on ~4,000 vehicles. Robot factories are built by humans, and the robots-build-robots loop needs exactly the hardest tasks (precision assembly, machining, construction). By 2031, robotics adds only ~5 points to S3's 51% Amdahl ceiling, with realized gains of ~40-50% versus 35-45% in S3. The physical clock of the robots themselves (hardware generations, field-hour reliability, certification, component capacity) is the new gate.
signposts: A humanoid maker publishes fleet-wide mean time between interventions or autonomy share (watch Agility's merger filings, Figure, Tesla Q3 2026 call)
Tesla reports an Optimus unit count in a shareholder letter, and Optimus does paid external work (2027)
1X NEO customer deliveries actually begin, and the share of Expert Mode teleoperation
ISO 25785-1 reaches DIS or FDIS stage; first uncaged humanoid deployments next to workers
UBTech Walker reaches its 80% human-productivity target (2027)
Zero-shot home or factory full-task success >90% on held-out sites (Figure, PI, DeepMind)
Tactile and contact sim-to-real transfer for multi-finger hands at production reliability
Humanoids doing a material share of assembly in a humanoid or EV factory (robots building robots), not just handling
China magnet export licensing (Nov 10 and Nov 27 2026 suspension deadlines); roller-screw capacity additions
Humanoids in aerospace production or test-stand operations moving beyond concept testing (Airbus, SpaceX/Tesla)
caveats: Shipment counts differ by analyst (Omdia vs IDC vs IFR vs company) because of definitions (full-size vs any humanoid, wheeled humanoid torsos, produced vs shipped vs deployed).
Many performance claims are company-reported (Figure, PI, Agility, Skild, DeepMind) without independent replication; Epoch's Feb 2026 review is the main independent assessment.
Some 2026 figures come only via secondary press or aggregator sites (Figure 1,000th unit, Tesla internal fleet estimates, Gemini Robotics 2 benchmark numbers).
Fleet projections to 2031 and 2035, labor-equivalence and S4 multipliers are my estimates, not sourced forecasts.
